messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] tuning trouble [research opportunity!]
parts:
On 11/1/13, 2:05 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On 10/31/2013 10:44 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>> It looks to me as if the problem I referred to in my previous post,
>> namely that only 1 of 3 chains seems to have moved around, is a result
>> of wildly different step sizes chosen by the tuner.
>>
>> Can anyone recommend a solution?
> I tried invoking with control=list(stepsize=0.0015, max_treedepth=13), but that doesn't seem to have fixed the
> stepsize. Do I want adapt_engaged=FALSE? I would still like the NUTS behavior.

You'll can still get NUTS with adapt_engaged=FALSE, but what
you won't get is a non-unit mass matrix estimated. This
won't be a big deal if the chain that worked had a mass
matrix that was similarly scaled in all dimensions, but could
be problematic otherwise.

One thing you might try now is upping the target acceptance rate
and starting from a less diffuse set of initializations.

Michael's busy improving our adaptation algorithms, which
we know to be highly variable as you report in other situations.
Hopefully over the next version or two of Stan, we'll roll out
something that's a little less variable and more reliable in its
convergence.

It seems to be a pretty wide-open research area that's related
to some of the online approaches to adaptation in machine learning,
particularly various forms of stochastic gradient descent. I don't
know if anyone has any kind of theoretical results at all related
to sampling vs. adaptation. If so, I'd love to hear about them.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] tuning trouble [research opportunity!]
parts:
> Is there a good way to recover the mass matrix? The only thing I could find was
> get_adaptation_info() which has it, but buried inside a string along
> with other pieces of information.
I'm not as familiar with Rstan, but that's pretty much how it's output from the underlying code.

> For the initial values, would drawing them from the one chain that
> seemed to work be a good idea or a bad idea? The main risk I can see
> is that this will be underdispersed and might not explore the solution
> space fully.

That's the problem -- it's really hard to verify when adaptation has gone wrong because
the curvature at the initial position was bad or the adaptation was too aggressive.
We're working on diagnostics that can provide some discrimination here, but until
then it's unfortunately a judgement call.

> Maybe there could be some kind of warning if different chains end up
> with radically different step sizes. I'm not sure how big that is,
> though I'm pretty sure 10^20 qualifies! OTOH, ending up with n_eff <
> 2 is already a pretty good clue that something has gone wrong.

The difficulty is in getting the chains to communicate with each other -- if they could
talk we'd just have them share adaptation info from the beginning. It's on
the very, very long to-do list.

Right now your best bet is to isolate the chains with clearly pathological behavior
and rerun from the same initialization but tweaked adaptation to see if you can
achieve better results.

parts:
On 11/6/13, 6:46 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> A couple of questions while I let it run without adaptation.
>
> On Sun, Nov 03, 2013 at 06:08:31PM -0500, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>>
>> On 11/1/13, 2:05 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>>> On 10/31/2013 10:44 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>>>> It looks to me as if the problem I referred to in my previous post,
>>>> namely that only 1 of 3 chains seems to have moved around, is a result
>>>> of wildly different step sizes chosen by the tuner.
>>>>
>>>> Can anyone recommend a solution?
>>> I tried invoking with control=list(stepsize=0.0015, max_treedepth=13), but that doesn't seem to have fixed the
>>> stepsize. Do I want adapt_engaged=FALSE? I would still like the NUTS behavior.
>>
>> You'll can still get NUTS with adapt_engaged=FALSE, but what
>> you won't get is a non-unit mass matrix estimated. This
>> won't be a big deal if the chain that worked had a mass
>> matrix that was similarly scaled in all dimensions, but could
>> be problematic otherwise.
>
> Is there a good way to recover the mass matrix? The only thing I could find was
> get_adaptation_info() which has it, but buried inside a string along
> with other pieces of information.

Not yet. We're working on making this easier, in part so a chain
can be restarted from where it left off.

>> One thing you might try now is upping the target acceptance rate
>> and starting from a less diffuse set of initializations.
>
> For the initial values, would drawing them from the one chain that
> seemed to work be a good idea or a bad idea? The main risk I can see
> is that this will be underdispersed and might not explore the solution
> space fully.

It'll help with convergence. You can always add noise around the
values that worked.

We've been considering various ways to use optimization (which is
super fast) for initialization, but it's not much help with hierarchical
models in their usual parameterizations, at least not without marginalizing
out some of the variables.

>> Michael's busy improving our adaptation algorithms, which
>> we know to be highly variable as you report in other situations.
>> Hopefully over the next version or two of Stan, we'll roll out
>> something that's a little less variable and more reliable in its
>> convergence.
>
> Maybe there could be some kind of warning if different chains end up
> with radically different step sizes. I'm not sure how big that is,
> though I'm pretty sure 10^20 qualifies! OTOH, ending up with n_eff <
> 2 is already a pretty good clue that something has gone wrong.

The other big research issue is how to combine adaptation info across
chains. One of the big problems is that if the posterior varies in
curvature, there's not a good target because the mass matrix changes with
location. But given that we're adapting a single global mass matrix (at
least in Euclidean HMC), there's no reason not to combine info across chains.

I somehow doubt different chains will adapt to different regions of
the posterior, but then it is a research problem.

- Bob

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] tuning trouble [update]
parts:
I finally got this to work by using values from the one good chain as
starting values for all.

The bad starting values generated likelihoods that were either very
large negative values or -Inf. I think the problem was that they were
just too unlikely to permit meaningful progression to better values
(most obviously for -Inf).

Inspecting the chains that didn't work showed that some key parameters
(all related to variance) in the bad chains were outside the range of
values explored by the one good chain. I tried editing the initial
values to put these values in a plausible range, but it didn't help (in
fact, in one case it moved the LL from large, finite negative value to
-Inf).

I never tried systematically generating initial values with lower
dispersion than the default; I was hoping my stop modifications would do
the trick. Pulling them all toward zero likely would not have worked,
since some of the failed chains started with sigmas that were too small.

I also noticed that I had specified
vector[J] beta_raw; // ordinary covariate coefficients
vector[J] theta_raw;
with
beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5); // special handling for intercept
theta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5);
for (j in 2:J) {
beta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
theta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
}
I thought having mismatched support on the first parameters might be a
problem, but specifying bounds for the parameters (probably not the
right thing to do...) didn't make a difference. Note that the posterior
for theta[1] (below) was substantially below -5. I suppose that's a
clue I need a different prior. There are probably scaling issues since
-5 or -500 for this parameter mean about the same thing, namely
Pr(monogamy)=0.

The resulting estimates were a bit odd, especially for the monogamy part
of the model. The intercept gave almost no probability of monogamy, but
the random person effects and the coefficients were all large.

Here are some of the key estimates:

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75%

beta[1] -0.42 0.02 0.20 -0.85 -0.54 -0.41 -0.28
sigma_alpha 0.50 0.01 0.14 0.21 0.41 0.51 0.61
sigma_beta[1] 0.88 0.05 1.17 0.02 0.22 0.52 1.06

theta are coefficients of the monogamy model, with theta[1] the
intercept. The theta are in 3 groups, with sigma_theta giving their
standard deviations. sigma_m_alpha is for person specific effects. It's
a logistic model. Attempting to estimate both cluster and individual
effects for monogamy seemed overly ambitious, and so I left the cluster
effects out of that part of the model.

The beta are for the count model, exponentiated to get lambda. beta[1]
is the intercept; sigma_alpha is for person effects and sigma_gamma for
clusters of persons (sigma_total and sigma_gamma_share were the targets
of estimation for stability).

For reference, here's the model:

/* outcome is mnDetail, an integer in [1, 10].
Our model is that there is some probability of being monogamous and some probability
thet mnDetail-1 is drawn from a poisson, with censoring at mnDetail = 10 (i.e., 11 or
more are reported as 10.
There are cluster effects, each cluster being all those recruited from a particular seed.
There are also individual effects for the poisson, but not the monogamy, model.
*/
data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of respondents
int<lower=0> J; //number of covariates
int<lower=0> NSD; // number of classes of beta for sd
int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J]; // beta[j, k] has sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
int<lower=0> NCLUSTER; //number of seeds
int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
matrix[N, J] x; // covariates
int<lower=1,upper=10> mnDetail[N]; // outcome
}
parameters {
/**** poisson model parameters ****/
vector[J] beta_raw; // ordinary covariate coefficients
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
vector[N] gamma_raw; // respondent effects
real<lower=0> sigma_total; // sqrt(individual + cluster variance)
real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD]; // sd for beta priors
real<lower=0,upper=1> gamma_share; // fraction of sigma_total^2 to gamma vs beta
/**** monogamy (1 inflation) model *****/
vector[J] theta_raw;
real<lower=0> sigma_theta[NSD]; // sd of priors
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_m_raw; // cluster effects _m_ for monogamy
real<lower=0> sigma_m_alpha; // sd for cluster effects
}
transformed parameters {
/*** poisson ****/
vector[J] beta;
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha;
vector[N] gamma;
real<lower=0> sigma_alpha; // cluster effects sd
real<lower=0> sigma_gamma; // respondent effects sd
/* monogamy */
vector[J] theta;
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_m;
/*start code */
sigma_alpha <- sqrt(1.0-gamma_share)*sigma_total;
sigma_gamma <- sqrt(gamma_share)*sigma_total;
for(ir in 1:J) {
beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
theta[ir] <- theta_raw[ir]*sigma_theta[SDClass[ir]];
}
alpha <- alpha_raw*sigma_alpha;
alpha_m <- alpha_m_raw*sigma_m_alpha;
gamma <- gamma_raw*sigma_gamma;
}
model {
vector[N] beta_x;
vector[N] theta_x;
sigma_total ~ cauchy(0, 5);
sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5); // special handling for intercept
theta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5);
for (j in 2:J) {
beta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
theta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
}
gamma_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
// gamma_share implicitly uniform(0, 1)
sigma_theta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
alpha_m_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
sigma_m_alpha ~ cauchy(0, 5);
for (n in 1:N) {
beta_x[n] <- (x[n] * beta)+alpha[iCluster[n]]+gamma[n];
theta_x[n] <- (x[n] * theta)+alpha_m[iCluster[n]];
if (mnDetail[n] == 1)
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1, theta_x[n]),
bernoulli_logit_log(0, theta_x[n]) + poisson_log_log(0, beta_x[n])));
else {
increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0, theta_x[n]));
if (mnDetail[n] < 10)
increment_log_prob(poisson_log_log(mnDetail[n]-1, beta_x[n]));
else
increment_log_prob(poisson_ccdf_log(8, exp(beta_x[n])));
}
}
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] tuning trouble [update]
parts:
A few general points.

Firstly, initialization in Stan is done in the unconstrained scale, so init=0 does not correspond to sigma=0 but rather sigma=0.

It is always dangerous to throw away initialization a because you can never tell if there are statistical issues that are biasing your samples. Now in practice bad inits in Stan are usually bad adaptation (as opposed to bad sampling), so instead of throwing inits out you should really be looking at the adaptation. Some features in the testing queue will make this easier soon, but for now you can try increasing the target acceptance probability or running first with a unit_e metric to avoid bad estimates of the variances messing up the sampler.

Of course adaptation is stressed by complex posteriors so improving your model can also help a lot. Tighter priors on variances tends to help, but also make sure your priors have a reasonable overlap with your posterior, as you noted.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] tuning trouble [update]
parts:
On 11/22/13, 2:02 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On 11/22/2013 12:39 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> A few general points.
>>
>> Firstly, initialization in Stan is done in the unconstrained scale, so init=0 does not correspond to sigma=0 but
>> rather sigma=0.
>
> I'm guessing the last sigma=0 should be sigma=1, going from an unconstrained to a constrained scale via exp.
>
> But I think you are saying I misunderstood how the init argument works. Say the first parameter is sigma, and the
> corresponding init value I give is 1. Are you saying that means the first value of sigma tried will be e? I thought
> the inits, as passed in by me and as returned by get_inits, were on the constrained scale.

Two different things are going on here.

If you take init=0, inits are all 0 on the unconstrained
scale, and then a parameter sigma constrained to be positive
will indeed be initialized at 1.

If you take init=2, then inits are uniform at random from [-2,2]
on the unconstrained scale.

If you specify an init file, they're on the constrained scale.

>> It is always dangerous to throw away initialization a because you can never tell if there are statistical issues that
>> are biasing your samples. Now in practice bad inits in Stan are usually bad adaptation (as opposed to bad sampling),
>> so instead
> My interpretation was that the likelihood could not be evaluated usefully (i.e., either NaN or nothing useful from the
> derivatives), so that adaptation never got a chance to start. How could adaptation be involved in the failure?

Both things can happen. You can start in a region where
Stan gets the gradients right and they're finite, but they're
so ill conditioned that it'll take a very long time to get to
the high mass region using our standard adaptation (which
Michael's working to make better, by the way).

This is arguably an adaptation problem in that what adaptation
should do is:

(a) find the high mass region of the posterior,

(b) estimate the mass (covariance) matrix or an approximation
from the high mass region, and

(c) find a good step sized based on the target acceptance rate.

Any of these can mess up, with the particular problem we usually
see is (a) being slow and thus biasing (b).

- Bob
